replies.author: @حقايقساده
replies.text:
Any alphabet is just a collection of shapes. You can decide for them to mean anything. When the Turks adopted the Latin script, they decided to make the letter C represent the sound that English readers associate with the letter J. But what's the fuss? You make the adjustment in your head, and that's that.

Latin has a number of redundant letters, like C, Q and X, which most European languages don't use to represent unique sounds. Are the c in crime, q in quality and k in kernel qualitatively different sounds? No. 

English has both V and W as distinct sounds, but most European languages don't, so one of them is usually redundant. German uses V as a redundant F. Arguably, you could even spell the English W with an O and it would have been the same sound. French does. 

These redundant letters are preserved as archaic relics in most languages that have apopted the Latin script, when they arguably could have been put to better use to represent sounds that are unique to their own languages. Why should English use the digraphs Ch, Sh and Th? Why not use some of these redundant letters to represent these sounds instead? Polish especially, being such a consonant heavy language, arguably should have done this instead instead of having the digraphs Sz, Cz and Rz.
